In [[mathematics]], specifically [[number theory]], '''Granville numbers''', also known as <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect numbers, are an extension of the [[perfect number]]s.

==The Granville set==
In 1996, [[Andrew Granville]] proposed the following construction of a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>\mathcal{S}</math>:<ref name="De Koninck (1998)">{{cite journal|vauthors=De Koninck JM, Ivić A|title=On a Sum of Divisors Problem|journal=Publications de l'Institut mathématique|year=1996|volume=64|issue=78|pages=9–20|url=http://www.emis.de/journals/PIMB/078/n078p009.pdf|access-date=27 March 2011}}</ref>

:Let <math>1\in\mathcal{S}</math>, and for any integer <math>n</math> larger than 1, let <math>n\in{\mathcal{S}}</math> if
::<math>\sum_{d\mid n, \; d<n,\; d\in\mathcal{S}} d \leq n.</math>

A Granville number is an [[element (mathematics)|element]] of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> for which equality holds, that is, <math>n</math> is a Granville number if it is equal to the sum of its proper divisors that are also in <math>\mathcal{S}</math>. Granville numbers are also called <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect numbers.<ref name="De Koninck 2009">{{Cite book |last=de Koninck |first=Jean-Marie |author-link=Jean-Marie De Koninck |translator-first = J. M. |translator-last=de Koninck |title=Those Fascinating Numbers |url=https://archive.org/details/thosefascinating0000koni/page/40/mode/2up |url-access=registration |publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] |location= Providence, RI |year=2008 |page=40 |isbn=978-0-8218-4807-4 |oclc=317778112 |mr=2532459 }}</ref>

==General properties==

The elements of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> can be {{math|<var>k</var>}}-deficient, {{math|<var>k</var>}}-perfect, or {{math|<var>k</var>}}-abundant. In particular, [[perfect number|2-perfect numbers]] are a proper subset of <math>\mathcal{S}</math>.<ref name="De Koninck (1998)" />

===S-deficient numbers===

Numbers that fulfill the strict form of the inequality in the above definition are known as <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-deficient numbers. That is, the <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-deficient numbers are the natural numbers for which the sum of their divisors in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is strictly less than themselves:

::<math>\sum_{d\mid{n},\; d<n,\; d\in\mathcal{S}}d < {n}</math>

===S-perfect numbers===

Numbers that fulfill equality in the above definition are known as <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect numbers.<ref name="De Koninck (1998)" /> That is, the <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect numbers are the natural numbers that are equal the sum of their divisors in <math>\mathcal{S}</math>. The first few <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect numbers are:

:6, 24, 28, 96, 126, 224, 384, 496, 1536, 1792, 6144, 8128, 14336, ... {{OEIS|A118372}}

Every [[perfect number]] is also <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect.<ref name="De Koninck (1998)" /> However, there are numbers such as 24 which are <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect but not perfect. The only known <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect number with three distinct prime factors is 126 = 2 · 3<sup>2</sup> · 7.<ref name="De Koninck 2009" />

===S-abundant numbers===

Numbers that violate the inequality in the above definition are known as <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-abundant numbers. That is, the <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-abundant numbers are the natural numbers for which the sum of their divisors in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is strictly greater than themselves:

::<math>\sum_{d\mid{n},\; d<n,\; d\in\mathcal{S}}d > {n}</math>

They belong to the [[complement (set theory)|complement]] of <math>\mathcal{S}</math>. The first few <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-abundant numbers are:

:12, 18, 20, 30, 42, 48, 56, 66, 70, 72, 78, 80, 84, 88, 90, 102, 104, ... {{OEIS|A181487}}

==Examples==
Every [[deficient number]] and every [[perfect number]] is in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> because the restriction of the divisors sum to members of <math>\mathcal{S}</math> either decreases the divisors sum or leaves it unchanged. The first [[natural number]] that is not in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is the smallest [[abundant number]], which is 12. The next two abundant numbers, 18 and 20, are also not in <math>\mathcal{S}</math>. However, the fourth abundant number, 24, is in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> because the sum of its proper divisors in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is:

:1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 8 = 24

In other words, 24 is abundant but not <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-abundant because 12 is not in <math>\mathcal{S}</math>. In fact, 24 is <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect - it is the smallest number that is <math>\mathcal{S}</math>-perfect but not perfect.

The smallest odd abundant number that is in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> is 2835, and the smallest pair of consecutive numbers that are not in <math>\mathcal{S}</math> are 5984 and 5985.<ref name="De Koninck (1998)" />
